Restriction enzyme. Bacterial nucleases that recognize and cleave DNA at specific palindromic sequences, typically four to eight base pairs long. They originated as bacterial immune defenses and have become indispensable molecular tools for cloning, sequencing, and genetic analysis. Restriction enzymes catalyze sequence-specific DNA cleavage, producing defined fragments. They bind palindromic double-stranded DNA sequences that read identically forward and reverse on complementary strands. The cleavage products can be blunt ends from direct cuts or sticky and cohesive ends from staggered cuts leaving overhangs. The specificity is exceptional. Some recognize six-base-pair sequences occurring statistically about every four thousand base pairs in random DNA, while eight-cutters are rare in a genome. These enzymes originated as part of restriction-modification systems in bacteria, where a methylase protects the host DNA while the restriction nuclease destroys foreign DNA. Common examples include EcoRI, which recognizes G-A-A-T-T-C, BamHI, which recognizes G-G-A-T-C-C, and PstI, which recognizes C-T-G-C-A-G. Hundreds of distinct restriction enzymes have been catalogued. Sticky-end compatibility enables insertion of one digest product into another, forming recombinant DNA. Different enzymes recognizing the same sequence are called isoschizomers, while neoschizomers recognize similar but slightly different sequences. Restriction enzymes were essential to modern molecular biology's emergence in the nineteen seventies. Their discovery transformed genetic engineering from theoretical possibility into practical reality. Scientists could now break DNA at known locations and reassemble it in new configurations. Though sequencing and direct gene synthesis have superseded them for some applications, restriction enzymes remain fundamental in molecular diagnostics, cloning, and teaching.
